h1:
Sisaket Street Food & Night Markets
Grilled, Fried & Local Sweets After Dark
intro: Once the sun drops, Sisaket switches into eat-and-walk mode. The night market behind the train station fires up its grills, charcoal smoke drifts down the lane, and the fryers start working overtime. On Saturdays there's a long walking street to graze your way through as well. We've done the legwork so you know where to start your evening meal, what to order, and which local sweets you simply can't find anywhere else.

blocks.html: Sisaket doesn't have street food on the scale of the big tourist cities, but the upside is that it's the real thing locals eat — still cheap, and carrying that southern-Isan mix of Khmer, Suay and Nyer culture that makes some dishes more unusual than your average night market. Evening meals here revolve mainly around the night market behind the train station, backed up by the Saturday walking street and the municipal fresh market, which still has food to grab in the late afternoon. We've broken it down by area and told you straight what each spot does best and when to go.

blocks.text: Night markets and evening grazing spots in town

blocks.html: If you're staying in Sisaket town, the main evening eating spots are all close together — a few minutes on foot or by car gets you there. Start at the night market behind the train station, which is open every day, then move on to the walking street if it happens to be a Saturday. We've listed them in order of convenience and when they're busiest.

items.name: Si Nakhon Lamduan Night Market (behind Sisaket train station)
items.blurb: The town's main night market, on the far side of the train station along Ratchakan Railway 3 Road, open every day. You can walk a long stretch covering savory dishes, grilled food, fried snacks, fruit and desserts. This is where Sisaket locals come to bag up dinner to take home — easy on the wallet, friendly atmosphere. If you only have one night, come here first.
items.meta: Behind the train station, Ratchakan Railway 3 Rd · open daily ~3.30pm–11.30pm
items.price: One-plate dishes ฿35–60 · grilled skewers ฿10–20 each

items.name: Sisaket Walking Street (Mali–Nong Khaen cultural market)
items.blurb: The biggest walking street in the province, held on Saturday evenings into the night. There's far more food than on weekdays — street food, local sweets, handmade goods and souvenirs. It's made for long, slow grazing, so if your trip lands on a Saturday, save that night for the walking street.
items.meta: Mali–Nong Khaen area, Mueang district · Saturdays only ~4pm–10pm

items.name: Municipal Fresh Market 1 (evening food zone)
items.blurb: A long-running fresh market in the middle of town on Khukhan Road. By day it's a wet market, but from late afternoon into evening there are stalls of ready-to-eat food — fried snacks, khanom jeen, made-to-order dishes and Thai sweets. Good for grabbing dishes to take back to your room or finding a snack before dinner.
items.meta: Khukhan Rd, Mueang Tai subdistrict, Mueang district · daytime into evening

items.name: Food court around the island park – Nong Kwang Did public park
items.blurb: In the evening, food carts and stalls line up along the waterside plaza in the middle of town. People come to walk and exercise, then pick up grilled food, fried snacks and fruit smoothies to eat by the water. It's a chiller vibe than the night market — good if you'd rather sit and eat in peace without the crush.
items.meta: Central public park, Sisaket town · evenings

items.name: Rotating flea markets and night markets around town
items.blurb: Sisaket has flea markets that rotate by day across different neighborhoods around town. Some nights it's a flea market selling goods mixed with food, other nights it leans street food. Ask your hotel which neighborhood has a market that night, and you'll get to eat like a local without going far.
items.meta: Rotating by area/day · ask your hotel

blocks.title: Line your nights up with the markets
blocks.html: The walking street only runs on Saturdays, while the night market behind the station is open every day. If you want both, try doing the walking street on Saturday night and saving the night market for another night — that way you cover both without overlap.

blocks.text: Grilled food you have to order at the night market

blocks.html: Grilled food is the star of Sisaket's night markets. Whichever way you walk you'll hit a charcoal grill, smoke wafting down the whole lane. Most of it is sold by the skewer or by the set, prices are gentle, and it's perfect for buying several things to share.

items: Grilled chicken & pork skewers — the classic grilled pairing with sticky rice. The grilled chicken is fragrant with herbs, the pork skewers cost just a few baht each. Stop at a stall with a queue and you'll get it fresh.
Grilled intestines & offal — a favorite for the spice crowd, dipped in hot jaew sauce. Crisp outside, soft inside, grilled intestines are the snack Isan folks order with their beer.
Grilled fish & prawns — freshwater fish stuffed with lemongrass and salt-grilled, fragrant and fresh. Plenty of stalls at the night market do this well, eaten with seafood dipping sauce or jaew.

Grilled bananas, khao jee & grilled sticky rice — homely sweet grills: khao jee (grilled sticky rice brushed with egg) and grilled sticky rice stuffed with banana or taro. Easy snacks to nibble while you walk.
Sun-dried pork & fried sun-dried beef — some stalls grill it, some fry it. Order it with sticky rice or plain rice and you're full. It keeps well, so it's a good thing to buy and take home.

blocks.text: Hot fried snacks at the night market

blocks.html: Walk a little past the grill zone and you'll hit the row of fried-food stalls, woks hot the whole time. The fried food here ranges from the standard stuff you'll find all over Thailand to local items that are harder to track down.

items: Fried chicken & fish-sauce chicken wings — fried fresh at the stall, crispy-skinned, great on their own or with sticky rice. This is the fried food that sells well at almost every market.
Fried bananas, sweet potato & taro — sweet fried snacks in crisp batter, fried fresh and hot, a few baht a bag. Easy to grab and eat on the move.
Fried spring rolls, fried wontons & fried meatballs — fried snacks on skewers with dipping sauce, the kind you eat as you walk. Kids love them.

Fried bugs & insects — the Isan oddity: crickets, silkworm pupae, giant water bugs, fried crisp and salted. If you're brave enough to try, it's a genuine local experience — though we'll be honest, it's not for everyone. Start with a little first.
Khao kriap pak mor & local fish cakes — some stalls make these fresh on the spot, with punchy fried fish cakes eaten with cucumber relish. A snack that's tastier than you'd expect.

blocks.title: Straight talk on raw and fermented food
blocks.html: Isan night markets often have koi, raw larb, raw pickled fish (pla som) and fermented giant water bug mixed in. If you're not used to raw or fermented food, go for the grilled and fried items that are fully cooked — it's safer. Raw freshwater fish in particular carries a liver-fluke risk, so if you want to try it, choose the cooked version.

blocks.text: Local sweets and desserts worth tasting

blocks.html: Sisaket has local sweets that are hard to find elsewhere, because it's a four-tribe province (Lao, Suay, Khmer and Nyer). Many of the sweets have roots in Khmer and genuinely local culture. If you spot them at the night market or walking street, don't walk past.

items.name: Khanom sao-ang (khanom pad)
items.blurb: A legendary Sisaket local sweet with Khmer roots — flour cooked down then grilled until fragrant, sweet, rich and soft. It's been honored as one of the province's signature local dishes. You'll find it at markets and cultural fairs; if you see it, try it.

items.name: Khanom nang led (khao taen)
items.blurb: Sticky rice pressed into discs, fried crisp and drizzled with cane syrup — sweet and crunchy. It's a Sisaket specialty and popular souvenir, good to snack on or carry home.

items.name: Khanom tod ma
items.blurb: An old-fashioned sweet with a funny name, made from local wild fruit that's grilled or steamed until fragrant — sweet and rich. It's hard to find these days, and plenty of younger Thais have never tried it.

items.name: Thai cart sweets — bua loy, khanom krok
items.blurb: The standard night-market desserts: bua loy in ginger syrup, hot khanom krok, khanom tuay and lod chong, a few baht a bag. A good way to round off your evening meal.

blocks.title: Some local sweets are seasonal
blocks.html: Sweets like sao-ang and tod ma aren't sold every day at every stall. Sometimes you'll only find them at the walking street, cultural fairs or specific vendors. If you really want to try them, ask people at the market or check the province's cultural-market page before you go.
If you have two nights in Sisaket town, here's an unhurried eating plan you can adjust to the day you arrive. If you're here on a Saturday, bump the walking-street night up to the front.

blocks.label: Night 1
blocks.title: Night market behind the train station

items.activity: Take a stroll at the central public park to work up an appetite
items.note: There are food carts by the water — grab a smoothie or some grilled food to whet your appetite first

items.activity: Head into Si Nakhon Lamduan night market behind the station
items.note: Start with the grills — grilled chicken, pork skewers, grilled intestines — ordered with sticky rice

items.activity: Move on to fried food and one-plate dishes
items.note: Fried chicken, grilled fish, then made-to-order dishes or noodles if you've still got room
Bua loy, khanom krok or seasonal fruit. Buy some sticky rice and sun-dried pork to take back for later tonight

blocks.label: Night 2
blocks.title: Walking street (if it's a Saturday) or a neighborhood market

items.activity: Head to Sisaket Walking Street in the Mali–Nong Khaen area
items.note: If it's not a Saturday, ask your hotel which neighborhood has a market that night instead

items.activity: Graze on street food and local sweets
items.note: Look out for khanom sao-ang, khanom nang led and the unusual grilled items you won't find on weekdays

items.activity: Find a proper place to sit and eat
items.note: Order som tam, larb and grilled chicken as your main meal, then carry on grazing on sweets
Khanom nang led, sun-dried pork or handmade goods from the walking street make good things to bring back

blocks.text: Eat your way through a Sisaket evening like a local

items: Carry cash and small notes — most cart vendors still don't take cards, and only some have PromptPay.
Go in the early evening, around 6pm to 8pm, when it's busiest — everything's out and the most stalls are open. Go too late and some start packing up.
Order a little from several stalls. Night markets are made for grazing rather than ordering a lot from one place.
Ask the price first if there's no sign, especially for grilled food sold by weight or for seafood, so there's no confusion when you pay.
If you're not used to raw or fermented food, choose the cooked grilled and fried items — just as safe and just as tasty.

blocks.title: If you're heading out to the border next
blocks.html: Plenty of people eat at the night market in town, then drive out the next day to Pha Mo I Daeng or Khao Phra Wihan National Park in the south of the province. We'll be honest: that border area has periods when it's closed or restricted, so always check the situation and whether the area is open before you set off, and have a backup plan ready.

faq.q: Where's the best place to eat at Sisaket's night markets?
faq.a: The main spot is the Si Nakhon Lamduan night market behind the train station, open every day around 3.30pm–11.30pm with everything from grilled and fried food to desserts. If you're here on a Saturday, add Sisaket Walking Street in the Mali–Nong Khaen area, where there's more food and far more local sweets than on weekdays.

faq.q: What time does Sisaket's night market open?
faq.a: The night market behind the train station (Si Nakhon Lamduan) is open every day, roughly 3.30pm to midnight. It's busiest from 6pm to 8pm, when the stalls are all out and the food is fresh. If you go very late, some vendors start packing up.

faq.q: Which Sisaket local sweets should I try?
faq.a: The most famous is khanom sao-ang (also called khanom pad), a Khmer-rooted local sweet that's grilled, sweet and rich — it's been honored as one of the province's signature local dishes. Next is khanom nang led (khao taen), a popular souvenir, and khanom tod ma, an old-fashioned sweet with a funny name. Some sweets are seasonal, so ask people at the market or check the Saturday walking street.

faq.q: Do I need cash at Sisaket's night markets?
faq.a: You should carry cash and small notes, because cart vendors and roadside grills mostly still take cash. Some have PromptPay, but not all. Having coins and small bills on hand makes things easier.

faq.q: Is the unusual food at Sisaket's night markets safe to eat?
faq.a: The cooked grilled and fried food is safe and tasty. As for raw and fermented items like raw koi, raw pickled fish or fermented giant water bug, if you're not used to them we'd suggest skipping them or choosing the cooked versions — raw freshwater fish in particular carries a liver-fluke risk. Fried insects count as a local specialty; you can try a little first.
